passage: For months after the bullying at his school in Hanoi, Bao went straight home each day. With the school counsellor he began weekly talks. On Wednesdays the counsellor helped him name what had happened and reminded him none of it was his fault. He joined a climbing club, where Lucia, a girl from the year above, taught him to belay, and where being scared and doing it anyway felt normal. By spring he had three friends he ate lunch with. A year later the counsellor asked if Bao would talk to the Year 7s. Bao stood in front of them for ten minutes. "If someone keeps making you feel small, tell one adult early," he said. "Don't wait like I did." A boy at the back nodded.

qa.q: Who taught Bao to belay at the climbing club?
qa.a: Lucia, a girl from the year above, taught Bao to belay.

qa.q: How did Bao feel at the climbing club, and what does it show?
qa.a: Bao felt more capable and less alone there, since being scared and doing it anyway began to feel normal.

qa.q: What else could Bao do to keep helping younger students, and why?
qa.a: Bao could offer to be a lunchtime buddy for Year 7s who feel left out, because early company and a trusted person make speaking up easier.

qa.q: How might the boy at the back of the room have felt?
qa.a: The boy probably felt understood and encouraged, since someone older spoke openly about waiting too long.

grounding: With help from a counsellor, sport and a small circle of supportive friends, the student regains confidence, and later helps younger students recognise bullying and speak up early.

passage:
The school's sports complex was mostly empty at 4 pm, except for the badminton court, where Keerthana was smashing shuttles harder than anyone in the under-16 group.

A year ago she had barely spoken in class. After months of being mocked by a group in her section, she'd started meeting the school counsellor, Mr. Manoj, every Thursday. He hadn't made it go away overnight. But together they'd worked out small steps: join one club, sit with two kind classmates, say one thing in class each day.

She picked badminton. The coach noticed her footwork. Her two lunch friends became four.

Now, this afternoon, a Class 6 girl came to the court edge, eyes wet. "Some girls keep laughing at my shoes."

Keerthana put her racquet down and sat beside her. "That's not okay. Come, let's go to Mr. Manoj right now. I'll come with you." In his room, Mr. Manoj listened, told the girl it wasn't her fault, and wrote down the names before the bell.

qa.q: What day did Keerthana meet the counsellor?
How might Keerthana have felt when the Class 6 girl came to her?
qa.a: She probably felt protective and a flash of recognition, remembering her own hurt, but now calm and confident enough to help.

qa.q: What else could Keerthana do to help younger students speak up early?
qa.a: She could offer to talk briefly at a junior assembly about how she got help, so younger students know whom to approach.

qa.q: How might the Class 6 girl see Keerthana's response?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and taken seriously, since an older student believed her and walked her straight to the counsellor.

grounding: Shows a student who rebuilt confidence through counselling, sport and supportive friends, and later helps a younger student recognise bullying and seek help early.

passage:
Dear Sudha,

You asked me last week how I got back to being "normal" after Class 8. I've been thinking about it, and I want to answer properly.

It wasn't one thing. When the boys in my section had spent months calling me names and I'd started skipping school, my parents took me to the school counsellor. I met her every week for a term. She helped me stop thinking it was something wrong with me.

Then football. Coach made me a defender, and being shouted at to "hold the line!" made me feel strong again. And three friends, Vikram, Rehmat and Paul, who just kept saving me a seat.

Now I'm in Class 11, and I help at the junior anti-bullying club every Thursday. Last week a Class 6 boy told me about someone stealing his lunch. I took him straight to the counsellor, who called his parents that afternoon.

Anand

qa.q: Which day does Anand help at the junior anti-bullying club?
How did football make Anand feel?
qa.a: Being a defender made Anand feel strong again, bringing back some confidence after months of feeling small.

qa.q: What else could Anand do at the club to help younger students speak up early?
qa.a: Anand could share a simple list of adults to approach, so a younger student knows exactly where to go the same day.

qa.q: How might the Class 6 boy have felt being taken straight to the counsellor?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and believed, since an older student took his problem seriously right away.

grounding: A letter describes a student regaining confidence through counselling, sport and supportive friends, and later helping younger students speak up early.
